Cluster 01 DRILL: Cell Signalling

H2 Biology 9477 · Book 3 · 8 questions · 130 marks · 19 parts · built on LOs 3(m), 3(n), 3(o) and 3(p) only

Answers sit directly under each part, hidden. Click Show answer only after you have said your full reasoning aloud for that part. Check (a) before you start (b); that is the point of the layout.

Rate your confidence before every reveal. A dashed line sits above each answer block. Say high, medium or guessed out loud before you click. A correct guess is not mastery, and the transcript needs to record which is which, because a right answer said hesitantly stays ACTIVE while a right answer said confidently moves on.

Eight questions, and eight is what the coverage produced. Cluster 1 carries exactly four learning outcomes, 3(m), 3(n), 3(o) and 3(p), and the study sheet teaches nine sections under them. Grouped by the concept that has to surface, those collapse into eight questions, each fusing at least five concepts. A ninth would have to repeat a primary concept, so there is no ninth. Nothing here is padding.

Question 2 is the one that matters most. 9477 Specimen Paper 1 Q22 prints a five-stage pathway and asks which stages show signal amplification and which show enzyme activation. Amplification is where one molecule causes many to be produced. Activation is where a molecule is switched on. They are different steps, chapter 3.1 never separates them, and if you have only learnt that cascades amplify you cannot answer it. Q2 gives you the real specimen diagram, then makes you count the amplification steps in a second cascade, then breaks the condition that makes amplification possible.

Seven of the eight questions open on a real figure or a real data table, because 38.3% of the 684 questions in the cell-signalling corpus are figure-led and data interpretation is the largest single archetype in Book 3. Every image is the actual picture from the paper or chapter it came from, not a redrawing. Two questions are multiple choice, Q2(a) and Q6(a), and in both you have to say whether every row is right and why, not find the odd one out. The letter on its own is worth almost nothing.

Reaches back into Books 1 and 2. Q1(a) sets a receptor against an enzyme, so the whole question needs Book 1 cold. Q1(b) needs hydrophobic R groups forming hydrophobic interactions with the fatty acid tails. Q5(a) needs membrane fluidity. Q6(a) needs a transcription activator from Book 2. Q8(a) and Q8(b) need Book 2's control of gene expression, because LO 3(m) words the cellular response as a change in gene expression. A Book 1 or Book 2 gap surfacing here is worth more than a clean Book 3 answer, so say it out loud when it happens.

Scope, so you do not waste an answer. Homeostasis, negative feedback, set point and diabetes all return zero hits in the 9477 syllabus, and 22.8% of the cell-signalling question bank tests those or tests excluded receptors. Nothing here does. Intracellular receptors are excluded in the wording of LO 3(m), so only two receptor types appear anywhere in this drill: the G-protein linked receptor and the receptor tyrosine kinase. Nothing from chapters 3.2, 3.3 or 3.4 appears either, because you have not studied them yet.

Traps deliberately planted, every one traceable to a real reject line, examiner comment or specimen question. Amplification confused with activation, which is Specimen P1 Q22 exactly. The GDP said to be phosphorylated to become GTP, which is the most repeated reject in this chapter's corpus. A receptor's binding site called an active site, and the enzyme vocabulary that follows it. Phosphorylation assumed always to activate, when the chapter's own figure has protein kinase A phosphorylating glycogen synthase to inhibit it. Yes/no comparisons of the two receptor types, rejected in writing by two schemes. Tyrosine kinase used interchangeably with tyrosine residue. Cyclic AMP treated as a ligand for a cell surface receptor, which caught over 40% of one cohort. Glucagon said to act on skeletal muscle, which is your own chapter's error on pages 36, 37 and 41. A data answer given without quoting the data.

Question 1 [16 marks]

(a) Fig. 1.1 shows a G-protein linked receptor in a cell surface membrane.

A student says that a hormone binding to its receptor and a substrate binding to its enzyme are the same event under two different names. Decide whether the student is right. [10]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Decide whether a hormone binding its receptor and a substrate binding its enzyme are the same event. [10]

1. The student is partly right and partly wrong. The binding is the same kind of event, but what happens next is not, because a receptor is not an enzyme and nothing is converted into a product.

Similarities, max 4:

2. Both receptor and enzyme have sites with specific 3D conformation which only molecules of complementary shape will fit into, and both hormone and substrate bind to specific sites, the receptor site and the active site, on receptor and enzyme respectively.

3. Both show high specificity in their interactions.

4. Temporary weak bonds such as ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions are formed between hormone and receptor and between enzyme and substrate during the interactions. In Fig. 1.1 these form at the signal-binding site. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1: non-covalent R-group interactions]

5. Both receptor and enzyme can be reused, that is, both remain unchanged at the end of the interaction.

Differences, point to point, max 5:

6. Site for binding: the receptor has a binding site, whereas the enzyme has an active site. An examiner comment records that a number of students referred to the NS protein binding to the receptor's active site, which implied that they incorrectly thought of the receptor as an enzyme. R: calling the site in Fig. 1.1 an active site.

7. Lowering of activation energy: the enzyme enables reactions to proceed faster by lowering activation energy, whereas the receptor does not.

8. Conformational change in the site for binding: the receptor changes shape upon binding of hormones, whereas the active site does not change shape upon binding of substrates, following the lock and key hypothesis.

9. Induced fit: the enzyme shows it, because as the substrate enters and binds to the active site, it induces a conformational change in the shape of the enzyme such that the substrate can fit even more snugly into the active site; the receptor does not.

10. Fate of the bound molecule: there are no changes to hormones after binding, and hormones dissociate from the receptor after activation of other proteins, whereas there are changes to substrate after binding, products formed, since the substrate is broken down or converted to product after reaction. The complex formed is a hormone-receptor complex rather than an enzyme-substrate complex.

11. Cofactors: cofactors may be required by an enzyme, whereas for a receptor cofactors are not required.

12. Function: the receptor's function is cell signalling, the enzyme's is catalysing biological reactions.

QWC: the answer must be clearly expressed using the correct terminology and communicated without ambiguity, with at least 1 similarity and 1 difference addressed. A related scheme rejects the term competitive inhibitor for Tamoxifen even though the mechanism is competition for a binding site, because a receptor is not an enzyme, so describe the mechanism rather than naming it.

(b) Insulin is a peptide hormone, and its receptor sits in the cell surface membrane rather than in the cytosol. Account for the position of the receptor, and for the way it is held there. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Why the insulin receptor sits in the membrane, and what holds it there. [6]

1. Insulin is a large molecule or protein which is polar or hydrophilic.

2. Therefore insulin is repelled by, or unable to pass through, the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer, so it needs to bind to a receptor at the extracellular domain or ligand-binding site to trigger an intracellular response.

3. A receptor in the cytosol would never be reached, so the receptor must be transmembrane, with an extracellular domain facing the exterior of the cell and an intracellular domain facing the cytoplasm of the cell.

4. The polypeptide is folded in such a way that the transmembrane region mainly consists of amino acids with hydrophobic R groups. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1: R-group chemistry decides where a residue sits]

5. These amino acids form hydrophobic interactions with the fatty acid tails of the phospholipids in the cell surface membrane, so the receptor is stably embedded in the cell surface membrane.

6. The polar and charged R groups interact with the hydrophilic polar phosphate heads of the membrane, which allows the receptor to function on both sides of the membrane, that is, to bind signal molecule in the extracellular environment and generate intracellular signals in the cytosolic environment.

The figure is the school's own Fig. 10, chapter 3.1 p. 14. The claim-to-be-tested framing in (a) is the extension. [INFERRED: extension, no official key] for the framing only. Archetype: compare and distinguish, run as an evaluate-level claim to be tested. Trap: enzyme vocabulary applied to a receptor. Active site, induced fit, lowering activation energy and competitive inhibitor are all rejected for a receptor. Second trap: giving only similarities, when the question turns on the differences. Concepts fused: (1) complementary 3D conformation as the shared binding principle; (2) non-covalent bonds at a binding site, traced back to Book 1 R groups; (3) binding site against active site as a named distinction; (4) activation energy as the thing an enzyme does and a receptor does not; (5) lock and key against a receptor that changes shape on binding; (6) induced fit as an enzyme-only property; (7) the fate of the bound molecule, product against dissociation unchanged; (8) reusability as a genuine similarity; (9) a hydrophilic ligand unable to cross the hydrophobic core; (10) hydrophobic R groups and hydrophobic interactions with fatty acid tails as the anchoring mechanism; (11) polar R groups against phosphate heads; (12) extracellular and intracellular domains as the reason a transmembrane protein can transduce.

Question 2 [14 marks]

(a) Fig. 2.1 shows five numbered stages in one example of cell signalling.

Which row correctly identifies the stages at which signal amplification and enzyme activation occur?

signal amplificationenzyme activation
A1, 2, 3, 4 and 52, 3, 4 and 5
B2 and 3 only4 and 5 only
C3 and 5 only2, 4 and 5 only
D4 and 5 only2 and 3 only

For every row, say whether it is correct and why. [6]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which stages show signal amplification and which show enzyme activation. MCQ key: C. [INFERRED: no official key, Cambridge has published no mark scheme for the specimen papers] [6]

1. The test is mechanical. Amplification happens wherever one activated enzyme molecule catalyses the production or modification of many product molecules. Enzyme activation happens wherever the step converts an inactive enzyme into an active one. Ask at each arrow whether the number of molecules increases.

2. Stage 1 is neither. It is ligand binding to a receptor, and a receptor is not an enzyme, so nothing is activated as an enzyme and nothing is produced in greater number.

3. Stage 2 is activation only. The activated receptor, through a G protein, activates adenyl cyclase. One enzyme molecule is switched on and the count does not rise.

4. Stage 3 is amplification. One adenyl cyclase molecule converts many ATP molecules into many cyclic AMP molecules.

5. Stage 4 is activation only. Cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A, switching on an enzyme without increasing molecule number at that step.

6. Stage 5 is both. One activated protein kinase A phosphorylates and activates many molecules of the next protein kinase, so the step amplifies, and because those kinases are switched on from inactive to active it is also enzyme activation.

7. C is correct, giving amplification at 3 and 5 only and activation at 2, 4 and 5 only. Both cells must be right for the mark.

8. A is wrong. It marks every stage as amplification, which is the belief that every step of a cascade amplifies. Stage 1 is ligand binding and stages 2 and 4 are switch-on events with no increase in number.

9. B is wrong. It puts amplification at 2 and 3 and activation at 4 and 5. Stage 2 does not amplify, and stage 2 is itself an activation step, which B omits.

10. D is wrong, and it is the mirror image of C. It swaps the two columns almost exactly, marking 4 and 5 as amplification and 2 and 3 as activation, which credits stage 4 with amplification when only one kinase is switched on, and calls stage 3 an activation when cyclic AMP is not an enzyme.

(b) A second cascade runs in a liver cell, in this order:

  • adrenaline binds its receptor
  • the receptor activates many G proteins
  • each G protein activates one adenylyl cyclase
  • each adenylyl cyclase converts many ATP molecules into many cyclic AMP molecules
  • cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A
  • protein kinase A phosphorylates many phosphorylase kinase molecules
  • each phosphorylase kinase activates many glycogen phosphorylase molecules

Count the amplification steps in that pathway and justify each decision. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Count the amplification steps in the adrenaline cascade. [4]

1. Four amplification steps.

2. The receptor activates many G proteins, so one activated receptor gives many activated G proteins. Amplification.

3. Each G protein activates one adenylyl cyclase. One to one, so this is activation, not amplification.

4. Each adenylyl cyclase converts many ATP molecules into many cyclic AMP molecules. Amplification.

5. Cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A. Activation, not amplification.

6. Protein kinase A phosphorylates many phosphorylase kinase molecules, and each phosphorylase kinase activates many glycogen phosphorylase molecules. Two further amplification steps.

(c) A drug shortens the time for which each activated relay protein stays in its active form. It does not change how many proteins the pathway contains. Predict the effect on the size of the cellular response, and name which requirement for amplification the drug has broken. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) A drug that shortens the active lifetime of every relay protein. [INFERRED: extension, no official key] [4]

1. The response gets smaller, even though every protein in the pathway is still present and still activates the next one.

2. Amplification needs two things, and the drug removes the second: presence of multiple steps in the transduction pathway, and persistence of proteins in the active form long enough to process numerous molecules of substrate before they become inactive again.

3. The number of steps is unchanged, so the drug has broken persistence of the active form.

4. The mechanism is catalytic turnover. An activated kinase amplifies only because while it stays active it phosphorylates many substrate molecules; cut its active lifetime and each activated enzyme processes fewer substrate molecules, so the number of activated products at each step falls towards the number at the step before and the pathway relays the signal without magnifying it.

Sources & concepts

Source: 9477 Specimen P1 Q22 (a, verbatim stem, figure, option table and key C; the specimen ships without a mark scheme, so the option-by-option reasoning is reconstructed and tagged); TMJC Prelim 2022 P1 Q24, key C (b, verbatim stem and key; the school answer table gives the key only, so the step-by-step justification is the extension); NYJC Prelim 2018 P1 Q19, key B (b, the same count applied to a shorter cascade); TJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q3dii [1] and RI Prelim 2023 P3 Q3b [2] (b, activation of one adenylyl cyclase results in the production of many cyclic AMP molecules, verbatim); NYJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q6a(ii) [3] (b, one adenylyl cyclase making many cAMP as the amplification argument, verbatim); EJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q6b [3] (b, each protein kinase phosphorylates and activates many protein kinases in the series, verbatim). The figure is the specimen's own, page 12. Part (c) is an extension built on the chapter's two conditions for amplification, 3.1 p. 22. Archetype: data and figure interpretation at the hardest tier, closed with a prediction. Trap: believing every step of a cascade amplifies, which produces option A. Second trap: swapping the two columns, which produces option D, because the two ideas have never been separated. Concepts fused: (1) signal amplification defined as one molecule causing many to be produced; (2) enzyme activation defined as an inactive enzyme being switched on; (3) the mechanical does-the-number-increase test; (4) ligand binding as neither of the two; (5) a step that is both at once, which is stage 5; (6) adenyl cyclase turnover as the classic amplification step; (7) counting amplification steps in an unfamiliar cascade; (8) the two requirements for amplification; (9) catalytic turnover and persistence of the active form as the mechanism under the requirement; (10) predicting response size from a change to turnover rather than to pathway length.

Question 3 [16 marks]

(a) A drug switches off every protein phosphatase in a liver cell and leaves the kinases untouched. Glucagon then binds to that cell. Predict what happens to the signal, and decide whether the drug makes the response larger, longer, or both. [8]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Every protein phosphatase in a liver cell is switched off. [INFERRED: extension, no official key] [8]

1. A kinase catalyses the transfer of phosphate group from ATP (or GTP) to the targeted protein, leading to its activation or inactivation, in phosphorylation. A protein phosphatase does the reverse, rapidly removing phosphate groups from proteins, in dephosphorylation.

2. Together the pair acts as a molecular switch in the cell, turning cellular activities on or off as required, and the activity of a regulated protein depends on the balance between active kinase molecules and active phosphatase molecules.

3. With the phosphatases off, that balance is pushed entirely towards the phosphorylated state. Every relay protein the cascade phosphorylates stays phosphorylated.

4. The response is therefore longer. The pathway cannot be returned to its inactive state, because dephosphorylation and inactivation of protein kinases and other relay proteins is what turns off the pathway when the signal molecule is no longer present, so glycogenolysis continues after glucagon has gone.

5. It is also larger, because amplification depends on persistence of proteins in the active form long enough to process numerous molecules of substrate. Removing the enzyme that ends that persistence lengthens the active lifetime of every kinase, so each one phosphorylates more substrate molecules and the number of activated products at each step rises.

6. So the answer is both, and the two effects have different causes: the response lasts longer because termination has been removed, and it is bigger because turnover per activated enzyme has risen.

7. There is a cost. Phosphatase activity allows protein kinases to be available for reuse so the cell can respond again to another extracellular signal. With no phosphatases the cell cannot reset, so it cannot respond to a second glucagon signal and loses its sensitivity to any further change.

8. One qualification, because phosphorylation does not always lead to the activation of a protein; in some cases, it can decrease a protein's activity. In this same pathway protein kinase A phosphorylates glycogen synthase to inhibit it, so with no phosphatase glycogen synthase also stays inhibited, and glycogenesis stays switched off as well.

(b) Three enzymes end a signal: protein phosphatase, the intrinsic GTPase activity of a G protein, and phosphodiesterase. Compare what each one acts on and what each one achieves, then rank them by how much of a glucagon pathway would still run if that one enzyme alone were missing. [8]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Compare the three termination enzymes and rank them. [8]

What each acts on, max 3:

1. Protein phosphatase activity catalyses the dephosphorylation and inactivation of protein kinases and other relay proteins, so its substrate is a phosphorylated protein and it works on the relay proteins throughout the pathway, impeding it downstream.

2. Intrinsic GTPase activity of G protein rapidly catalyses hydrolysis of bound GTP to GDP, inactivating the G protein, so its substrate is a nucleotide bound to the G protein itself and it works at a single point, immediately after the receptor.

3. Phosphodiesterase activity catalyses the conversion of cAMP to AMP, so its substrate is a second messenger, not a protein, and it works between the effector enzyme and the first kinase, decreasing the cyclic AMP concentration.

Contrasted on two further axes, max 2:

4. Where the enzyme lives: the GTPase is built into the G protein itself, so the switch carries its own off-switch, whereas the phosphatase and the phosphodiesterase are separate enzymes that must find their substrates.

5. What is reset: the phosphatase allows protein kinases to be available for reuse, the GTPase returns the G protein to its inactive GDP-bound form and lets the effector return to its original inactive state, available for reuse, and the phosphodiesterase simply removes the second messenger, leaving the proteins as they were.

The ranking, max 3:

6. Losing the intrinsic GTPase leaves the most of the pathway running. The G protein remains permanently in the GTP-bound active form and keeps stimulating adenylyl cyclase, so every step downstream continues to be fed, and the pathway runs even after the ligand dissociates from the receptor. This is exactly the mutation that produces constitutive signal transduction.

7. Losing phosphodiesterase is next. cAMP levels will increase further, which in turn will activate PKA, so the kinase arm stays driven, but the phosphatases still work, so individual relay proteins can still be switched off and the cell retains a partial brake.

8. Losing protein phosphatase leaves the least running, in the sense that it acts last. The upstream steps still switch themselves off, since the G protein still hydrolyses its own GTP and cAMP is still destroyed, so the signal at the top ends normally; what persists is the already phosphorylated tail of the cascade. The ranking follows position in the pathway, not importance of the enzyme: the earlier the terminating enzyme acts, the more of the pathway keeps running without it.

Sources & concepts

The three termination mechanisms and the two conditions for amplification are chapter 3.1 pp. 22 and 24. Both parts are extensions in their framing. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain closed with a ranking, which is LO 3(o) tested as written, that is, kinases and phosphatases inside amplification specifically. Trap: treating phosphorylation as always activating. Page 10 of the chapter says it activates the protein, page 12 corrects it, and the chapter's own glucagon figure has protein kinase A phosphorylating glycogen synthase to inhibit it. Second trap: answering that the response is only longer, and missing that removing the brake also raises turnover per enzyme. Concepts fused: (1) the kinase definition with its phosphate source; (2) the phosphatase definition; (3) the pair as a molecular switch and the balance between them; (4) phosphorylation that inhibits rather than activates; (5) termination as the reason a cell can respond a second time; (6) reuse of relay proteins; (7) persistence of the active form as the link from termination back to amplification; (8) the three named termination enzymes and their three different substrates; (9) an enzyme that is intrinsic to its target against enzymes that are separate; (10) constitutive signalling as the consequence of a failed GTPase; (11) ranking lesions by position in a dependency chain rather than by severity.

Question 4 [16 marks]

(a) Fig. 4.1 shows part of a signal transduction pathway. W is the signal molecule, X is the receptor before binding, Y is the phosphorylated intracellular region of the receptor, and Z is a small non-protein molecule.

Describe the events from W binding to X until Y activates an intracellular pathway, then account for the fact that it is Z, and not W, that carries the signal through the cytosol. [8]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) From W binding X to the activation of an intracellular pathway, and why Z carries the signal. [8]

The reception and transduction events, max 4:

1. Binding of ligand W, which is complementary in shape to the ligand binding site of receptor tyrosine kinase (X), causes the two receptor subunits to dimerise, causing a conformational change in the intracellular domain of the receptor.

2. This activates the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the intracellular domain which cross-phosphorylates the tyrosine residues at Y.

3. Phosphorylated Y will provide a docking site for relay proteins to transduce signals. In Fig. 4.1 the relay protein is the cytosolic enzyme drawn as activated, which binds a specific phosphorylated tyrosine and is activated by undergoing a conformational change.

4. That activated enzyme then cleaves a membrane phospholipid, releasing Z into the cytosol.

Why Z and not W, max 4:

5. Z is a second messenger. Its role is to diffuse throughout the cytoplasm and to activate downstream proteins, enzymes or relay molecules.

6. W cannot do that job, because W is a large or hydrophilic molecule and is unable to pass through the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer, which is why it binds a receptor at the surface in the first place. The original signal molecule is not physically passed along the pathway; what travels inward is a conformational change, and then a new molecule.

7. Z can do it because second messengers are small, non-protein, water-soluble molecules or ions, so they can readily spread throughout the cytosol by diffusion and reach targets far from the point on the membrane where the signal arrived.

8. Z also binds and induces a conformational change in a downstream protein, thus activating it, which in Fig. 4.1 is the protein drawn as activated that then opens the channel in the membrane, so the signal is passed on or relayed to the next relay protein during signal transduction.

(b) Cyclic AMP, inositol trisphosphate and calcium ions all act as second messengers. Compare the three, then judge which single property of a second messenger does the most work in a signalling pathway. [8]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Compare cyclic AMP, inositol trisphosphate and calcium ions, then judge. [8]

Shared, max 2:

1. All three are small, non-protein, water-soluble molecules or ions that transmit the message carried by the extracellular signal molecule, the first messenger, into the target cell's interior.

2. For all three, binding of the first messenger stimulates an increase in the concentration of second messengers, and because a large variety of relay proteins are sensitive to the cytosolic concentration of second messengers, that rise alters the behaviour of the relay proteins. All three therefore enable cells to mount a large-scale, coordinated response following stimulation by a single extracellular signal molecule.

Contrasted, point to point, max 4:

3. Where each is made or released. Cyclic AMP is synthesised from ATP by adenylyl cyclase, an enzyme embedded in the plasma membrane; IP3 is produced by cleavage of a membrane phospholipid by phospholipase C; calcium ions are not synthesised at all but released from the endoplasmic reticulum through an IP3-gated calcium channel that IP3 binds and opens.

4. Chemical nature. Cyclic AMP is a modified nucleotide derived from ATP, IP3 is a small phosphorylated ring molecule, and calcium is an ion. Note that DAG, produced alongside IP3, is a lipid and not a relay protein, and it stays in the membrane rather than diffusing.

5. What each activates. Cyclic AMP's immediate effect is usually activation of a serine/threonine kinase called protein kinase A; IP3 acts on a gated ion channel; calcium acts on calcium-binding relay proteins.

6. How the signal is ended. Cyclic AMP is destroyed, because phosphodiesterase converts the cAMP to AMP; calcium is removed from the cytosol rather than destroyed, which works because its concentration in the cytosol is normally much lower than the concentration outside the cell, so a brief increase is a usable signal against a quiet background.

The judgement, max 2:

7. The property that does the most work is being small and water-soluble, and therefore freely diffusible, because every other role depends on it. Diffusibility is what lets a signal received at one point on the membrane reach relay proteins throughout the cytosol and the organelles, which is what makes a large-scale, coordinated response possible.

8. Being non-protein matters for a different reason and is the second candidate: a protein relay would have to be synthesised by transcription and translation, which is slow, whereas a second messenger is produced in large numbers by one enzyme in a single catalytic step, which is where the amplification comes from. So diffusibility buys reach and non-protein nature buys speed and number. R: naming cyclic AMP and stopping, since LO 3(n) asks for roles and nature.

Question 5 [16 marks]

(a) Fig. 5.1 outlines the response of a liver cell to glucagon. Glucagon itself never enters the cell.

Account for the fact that enzyme Q, which sits on the inner face of the membrane, is switched on, and state exactly what happens to the GDP carried by the G protein. [9]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) How enzyme Q on the inner face is switched on, and what happens to the GDP. [9]

Reception, max 2:

1. Glucagon binds to the extracellular binding site of the receptor, which is complementary in shape and charge to it, and binding of the signal molecule results in a conformational change in the GPCR and activates the GPCR.

2. Glucagon cannot cross the membrane, because it is a large, hydrophilic peptide hormone that cannot pass through the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer of the cell surface membrane, so the conformational change, not the hormone, is what reaches the inside.

The G-protein switch, max 5:

3. The G protein functions as a molecular switch that is either on or off, depending on whether GDP or GTP is attached, and when GDP is bound the G protein is inactive.

4. The activated receptor now has an increased affinity for the G protein, so the cytoplasmic side of the activated GPCR binds to an inactive G protein.

5. A GTP molecule displaces the GDP molecule, activating the G protein. This is an exchange, not a phosphorylation. R: saying the GDP is phosphorylated to become GTP. The binding of GDP is via weak interactions, which is precisely what facilitates the exchange between GDP and GTP.

6. The GTP-bound subunit dissociates from the GPLR and diffuses along the membrane, which it can do because the cell surface membrane is fluid. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1: lateral diffusion of membrane proteins]

7. It then binds a target protein or effector, usually an enzyme, thereby altering target protein activity, which initiates a cascade of signal transduction events. In Fig. 5.1 that effector is enzyme Q, and active G-protein binds to and causes a conformational change to enzyme Q, activating it.

Shut-off, max 2:

8. The intrinsic GTPase activity of the G protein soon hydrolyses its bound GTP to GDP, so the G protein is inactive again.

9. The signal molecule dissociates from the GPLR and the effector returns to its original inactive state, available for reuse, which is why a liver cell can respond again to a later glucagon signal.

(b) In one family, liver cells break down glycogen even when no glucagon is present. Suggest two different single changes that would produce this, and decide which of the two would be harder to correct with a drug that blocks the glucagon binding site. [7]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Two mutations that give glycogen breakdown with no glucagon, and which is harder to block. [7]

1. Change one, in the receptor. A gain of function mutation in the gene which codes for the receptor produces a hyperactive receptor which binds to and activates the G protein permanently or continuously to trigger the signal pathway, even with no ligand bound.

2. Change two, in the G protein. A gain of function mutation in the gene which codes for the G protein produces hyperactive G proteins which bind to and activate adenylyl cyclase permanently. The commonest specific version is a failure of the GTPase, where GTPase in G protein fails to hydrolyse GTP to GDP, so the G protein remains permanently in the GTP-bound active form and keeps stimulating adenylyl cyclase, giving constitutive signal transduction.

3. In either case the consequence is the same: adenylyl cyclase keeps converting ATP to cyclic AMP, cyclic AMP keeps activating protein kinase A, and the cascade ends in activated glycogen phosphorylase, so glycogenolysis continues and glucose is released into the blood when it is not needed.

4. The G-protein mutation is harder to correct with a drug that blocks the glucagon binding site.

5. A binding-site blocker acts at the receptor, so with the receptor mutation the drug is still acting at the mutated component. It occupies the site the hormone would use, and if the mutation lies in the ligand-binding region the blocker can hold the receptor in a conformation that no longer activates the G protein.

6. With the G-protein mutation the drug is acting upstream of the lesion. The receptor is not the faulty component, so blocking it changes nothing, because the G protein is already in its active GTP-bound form without any input from the receptor.

7. The general rule, which is the mark here: an inhibitor can only switch off the part of a pathway that lies downstream of where it acts. To stop the G-protein version you would have to target the G protein itself or a step below it, for example an inhibitor of adenylyl cyclase, so the second messenger is not synthesised.

Source: School Prelim 2023 P1 Q24, key B, correct in 90.68% of the cohort (a, verbatim figure and stem; enzyme Q is adenylyl cyclase and second messenger R is cyclic AMP); TJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q3di [2] (a, the conformational change and GTP displacing GDP, verbatim); YIJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q7c [3] (a, the subunit dissociating and translocating along the membrane to adenylyl cyclase, verbatim); TMJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q9b [2] (a, the active G protein binding and causing a conformational change to enzyme P, verbatim); ACJC Prelim 2013 P2 Q6a [2] and NJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q8ai [3] (a, the displacement of GDP with GTP, verbatim); RI Prelim 2021 P1 Q24, key B (a, GDP is exchanged with GTP to activate the G protein and GDP is not phosphorylated, and the binding is via weak interactions to allow the exchange, verbatim); TMJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q9c [3] (a, why glucagon cannot cross the bilayer, verbatim); NYJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q6b [2] (b, the two gain of function mutations, verbatim); MI Prelim 2016 P1 Q26 and PJC Prelim 2017 P1 Q21, key D (b, the failed GTPase as the cause of constitutive signalling, verbatim); ACJC Prelim 2021 P2 Q9b [4] and ACJC Prelim 2024 P3 Q4(b) (b, blocking a receptor to stop the downstream cascade, and inhibitors of adenylyl cyclase, verbatim). The figure is the school's own 2023 Paper 1 Q24. The choice between the two mutations in (b) is the extension. [INFERRED: extension, no official key] for the ranking. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain on a figure, closed with a drug-target judgement. Trap: saying the GDP is phosphorylated to become GTP. This is the single most-repeated reject in the chapter 3.1 corpus, carried explicitly by two different schools. GTP displaces GDP and nothing is phosphorylated at that step. Second trap: forgetting that the G protein carries its own off-switch, so the pathway looks as if it needs an external terminator. Concepts fused: (1) complementary binding at an extracellular site; (2) why a peptide hormone cannot enter; (3) the conformational change as the thing that crosses the membrane; (4) the GDP or GTP occupancy as the on and off states of a molecular switch; (5) increased affinity of the activated receptor for the G protein; (6) GTP displacing GDP, and the reject that goes with it; (7) weak interactions as the reason the exchange is possible; (8) lateral diffusion in a fluid membrane, from Book 1; (9) the effector as a separate membrane enzyme; (10) intrinsic GTPase as a built-in terminator; (11) reuse of the receptor and effector; (12) constitutive activation by two different lesions; (13) the rule that an inhibitor only controls what lies downstream of it.

Question 6 [18 marks]

(a) Four proteins were isolated from a human cell and tested for the presence of three domains. Table 6.1 shows the results.

Table 6.1

protein Wprotein Xprotein Yprotein Z
transmembrane domain,++,
DNA binding domain,,,+
enzymatic domain+,+,

Key: + domain is present,, domain is absent.

Which row correctly identifies the four proteins?

protein Wprotein Xprotein Yprotein Z
AG-protein linked receptorG proteintyrosine kinase receptortranscription activator
BG proteintyrosine kinase receptorG-protein linked receptortranscription activator
Ctranscription activatorG-protein linked receptortyrosine kinase receptorG protein
DG proteinG-protein linked receptortyrosine kinase receptortranscription activator

For every row, say whether it is correct and why. [6]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Identify four proteins from their domains. MCQ key: D. [6]

1. Read the table as a set of requirements. A cell surface receptor must have a transmembrane domain, an enzyme must have an enzymatic domain, and a transcription activator must have a DNA binding domain.

2. Protein W has an enzymatic domain only. It is the G protein: it sits on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane rather than spanning it, so no transmembrane domain, and it carries intrinsic GTPase activity, which is the enzymatic domain.

3. Protein X has a transmembrane domain only. It is the G-protein linked receptor: it spans the membrane as seven α-helices, and it has no enzymatic activity of its own, which is exactly why it needs a separate G protein.

4. Protein Y has both a transmembrane domain and an enzymatic domain. It is the tyrosine kinase receptor, the one receptor here that possesses enzymatic activity, because its cytoplasmic part functions as an enzyme known as tyrosine kinase.

5. Protein Z has a DNA binding domain only. It is the transcription activator, which works inside the nucleus and so needs neither a transmembrane domain nor a catalytic one. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 2 LO 2(i): activators bind control elements and increase transcription]

6. D is correct. A is wrong because it makes W a GPLR, which would need a transmembrane domain W does not have, and makes X a G protein, which would need an enzymatic domain X does not have. B is wrong because it makes X a tyrosine kinase receptor, which needs both a transmembrane and an enzymatic domain, whereas X has only one, and it makes Y a GPLR, which has no enzymatic domain, whereas Y has one. C is wrong because it makes W a transcription activator, which would need the DNA binding domain that only Z has, and makes Z a G protein, which would need an enzymatic domain. Only D satisfies every row of Table 6.1 at once.

(b) Fig. 6.1 shows tyrosine kinase signalling at a cell surface membrane, in four stages left to right.

Describe what happens at each of the three arrows in Fig. 6.1, then account for the fact that one activated receptor of this type can start several different pathways at once, while one activated G-protein linked receptor starts one. [8]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) The three arrows in Fig. 6.1, and why one RTK starts several pathways. [8]

Arrow one, max 2:

1. The ligand binds to the extracellular ligand-binding site of a subunit, which is complementary in shape to it. Before the signal molecule binds, the receptor exists as two individual polypeptide subunits.

2. This gives receptor aggregation, where the two subunits associate closely, and dimerisation, where they form a dimer, causing a conformational change in the intracellular domain of the receptor.

Arrow two, max 3:

3. Dimerisation leads to the activation of the tyrosine kinase activity of the receptor.

4. The result is autophosphorylation, in which each kinase domain adds a phosphate from an ATP molecule to a tyrosine on the tail of its own or the other polypeptide subunit, which is the cross-phosphorylation drawn as the six P groups.

5. Note the wording. Tyrosine kinase is the enzyme and a tyrosine residue is the amino acid that gets phosphorylated, and an examiner comment records that many used the terms interchangeably. R: dimerisation of tyrosine kinase.

Arrow three, max 1:

6. The fully activated receptor binds cytoplasmic relay proteins, and each relay protein recognises and binds to a specific phosphorylated tyrosine, becoming activated by undergoing a conformational change. R: intracellular proteins, where relay proteins or protein kinases is wanted.

Why several pathways, max 2:

7. Multiple transduction pathways can be triggered by the activation of one RTK, as each phosphorylated tyrosine is recognised by a different relay protein, so several different cellular responses are generated from a single ligand-binding event, and relay proteins bound to the tyrosine kinase receptor activate different downstream pathways simultaneously.

8. The receptor in Fig. 5.1 cannot do this. It carries one intracellular site, the G-protein binding site, and the activated G protein binds one target protein, so the signal leaves the receptor by a single route. The structural difference, several phosphotyrosines against one G-protein site, is the functional difference.

(c) Give four differences between a G-protein linked receptor and a receptor tyrosine kinase, stating each difference positively on both sides. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Four differences, stated positively on both sides. [4]

1. Type of receptor: the GPLR is a single polypeptide chain, whereas the RTK exists as 2 polypeptide chains.

2. Structure of receptor: the GPLR consists of 7 α-helices transmembrane region and an intracellular binding site for G protein, whereas the RTK consists of 1 α-helix transmembrane region and an intracellular tail containing tyrosine kinase and multiple tyrosine residues.

3. Events on ligand binding: for the GPLR there is a conformational change of receptor resulting in activation of G protein, where GTP replaces bound GDP on G protein, whereas for the RTK there is dimerisation upon ligand binding and a conformational change resulting in activation of tyrosine kinase, followed by autophosphorylation or cross-phosphorylation of tyrosine residues in the cytoplasmic domain of the receptor.

4. Second messenger: GPLR signalling involves production of cAMP as a second messenger, whereas RTK signalling does not involve a second messenger, and GPLR signalling involves activation of adenylyl cyclase, whereas RTK signalling does not involve adenylyl cyclase.

R: yes/no comparisons. A scheme rejects the form GPLR does not have phosphorylated tyrosine residues while TKR has phosphorylated tyrosine residues, and wants a point-to-point structural difference with both sides stated positively.

Question 7 [18 marks]

(a) Table 7.1 shows blood glucose concentration and blood insulin concentration in one person after a glucose-rich meal eaten at 07.00.

Table 7.1

10.004.45110

12.004.570

With reference to Table 7.1, describe and explain the relationship between the two concentrations. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) The relationship between blood glucose and blood insulin after a glucose-rich meal. [4]

1. As the blood glucose concentration increases, the blood insulin concentration increases, that is, there is a positive correlation, and the insulin curve then follows the glucose curve down.

2. Supporting data quote: at 07.00 the blood glucose concentration was 4.3 mmol dm⁻³ and the blood insulin concentration was 30 pmol dm⁻³, while at 08.00 the blood glucose concentration was 6.2 mmol dm⁻³ and the blood insulin concentration was 280 pmol dm⁻³. Data must be quoted, because relevant supporting data must be quoted and answers are rejected without the quote.

3. The increase in blood glucose concentration causes the release of insulin from the pancreas, specifically from the β cells of the islets of Langerhans.

4. Insulin causes the blood glucose concentration to return back to the set point, because it increases the permeability of target cells to glucose and stimulates the conversion of glucose to glycogen, that is, glycogenesis. Supporting quote: glucose fell from 6.2 mmol dm⁻³ at 08.00 to 4.45 mmol dm⁻³ at 09.00 while insulin fell from 280 pmol dm⁻³ at 08.00 to 120 pmol dm⁻³ at 09.00. One scope note on that verbatim wording: set point returns zero hits in the 9477 syllabus, so write it as returns to its original concentration and keep the marks in the mechanism.

(b) Fig. 7.1 shows the signal transduction pathway in an adipose cell in response to insulin.

Insulin and glucagon are both peptide hormones and both reach cells in the same body, yet they bind different classes of receptor and have opposite effects on blood glucose concentration. With reference to Fig. 7.1 and your own knowledge, account for both facts. [10]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Why two peptide hormones use different receptor classes and have opposite effects. [10]

Why both must use a cell surface receptor, max 2:

1. Both are peptide hormones, so both are large and hydrophilic, and both are unable to diffuse across the hydrophobic core of the cell surface membrane. Each therefore binds a transmembrane cell surface receptor, and neither reaches the cytosol itself.

Why the receptor classes differ, max 4:

2. The class is not a property of the hormone, it is a property of the binding site the target cell provides. Target cells have cell surface receptors specific for the hormone, and the binding sites of receptors are complementary in shape to it. Insulin and glucagon have different 3D conformations, so they are recognised by different receptors, and those receptors happen to belong to different classes.

3. Insulin binds the insulin receptor, which is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Binding activates its tyrosine kinase activity, resulting in autophosphorylation, and relay proteins bind to specific phosphorylated tyrosines and are activated. In Fig. 7.1 that route runs through P13K, PIP3, protein kinase 1 and protein kinase 2.

4. Glucagon binds a specific G-protein linked receptor, which activates a specific G protein, which activates adenylyl cyclase, whose active form catalyses the synthesis of large amounts of intracellular cAMP from ATP; cAMP binds to and activates protein kinase A.

5. So the two differ at the first transduction event: GTP displaces GDP in one and autophosphorylation happens in the other, and only the glucagon route uses a second messenger.

Why the effects are opposite, max 4:

6. Insulin lowers blood glucose. Cytoplasmic vesicles carrying GLUT4 glucose transporters are stimulated to migrate to and fuse with the plasma membrane, increasing the number of glucose transporters so the rate of glucose uptake via facilitated diffusion rises. This is the arrow in Fig. 7.1 from protein kinase 2 to GLUT4, and the dashed arrow showing glucose entering the cell. Insulin also activates glycogen synthase, driving glycogenesis, the synthesis of glycogen from glucose, and inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

7. Glucagon raises blood glucose. The phosphorylations that follow protein kinase A end in glycogenolysis, the breakdown of glycogen to glucose, while the same kinase phosphorylates glycogen synthase, inhibiting its catalytic activity and so preventing glycogenesis. Glucagon also stimulates gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from a non-carbohydrate precursor, in liver cells, and the glucose formed diffuses into the bloodstream.

8. The two are antagonistic hormones which oppose each other's action, and it is the ratio of the amounts of these two hormones that determines the net effect, not their absolute amounts. Blood glucose is detected by the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas: high glucose stimulates β cells to secrete more insulin, low glucose stimulates α cells to secrete more glucagon.

9. The deep reason the effects are opposite is that the response proteins differ, not that the signalling machinery differs. One cascade ends on glycogen synthase in its active form and GLUT4 in the membrane, the other ends on glycogen phosphorylase in its active form and glycogen synthase inhibited. Note that the same enzyme, glycogen synthase, is the target of both, activated by one hormone and phosphorylated to inhibit it by the other, which is a clean demonstration that phosphorylation does not always lead to the activation of a protein.

(c) A student writes that glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis in the liver and in skeletal muscle. Decide whether that is right, and account for your decision. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Does glucagon stimulate glycogenolysis in skeletal muscle as well as in liver? [INFERRED: the school notes contradict themselves here, and no scheme in the corpus settles it] [4]

1. The student is wrong. Write liver, and only liver, for glucagon.

2. Skeletal muscle has no glucagon receptor. A cell only responds to a signal for which it possesses the correct receptor, since target cells have cell surface receptors specific for the ligand, so glucagon cannot be detected by a muscle cell at all and no signal transduction occurs.

3. Even if the glycogen were broken down, muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so the glucose released cannot leave the cell and cannot raise blood glucose concentration. Glucagon's whole function is to raise the concentration of glucose in the blood, which muscle glycogen cannot do.

4. Your own chapter states the wrong version on pages 36, 37 and 41 and the right one on page 34, where it correctly restricts glucagon to hydrolysis of liver glycogen. Adrenaline is the hormone that does act on muscle by the same GPLR and cyclic AMP route, which is probably where the confusion starts, and the muscle glucose is then used inside the muscle cell rather than exported.

Question 8 [16 marks]

(a) Fig. 8.1 shows the IL6 signalling pathway. IL6, a cytokine, binds to its receptor IL6R, and the complex then binds gp130, which works in the same way as a receptor tyrosine kinase. The tyrosine kinase carried on gp130 is called JAK.

Explain how IL6, which stays outside the cell throughout, changes which proteins that cell makes. [8]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) How IL6, which never enters the cell, changes which proteins the cell makes. [8]

1. IL6 is hydrophilic or water-soluble and so cannot pass through the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer of the cell surface membrane. Since it binds an extracellular receptor, it cannot act directly on the DNA in the nucleus, so the message must be carried inward by a chain of proteins.

2. IL6 binds to IL6R, and the IL6-IL6R complex then binds to gp130.

3. gp130 dimerises, leading to the activation of JAK, the tyrosine kinase, resulting in cross-phosphorylation, in which each JAK adds a phosphate to the other.

4. JAK phosphorylates a tyrosine residue on the cytoplasmic tail of gp130 of its own subunit, and gp130 is fully activated. Those phosphotyrosines are the docking sites.

5. JAK phosphorylates STAT3, and phosphorylation of STAT changes its conformation so that it is complementary in shape and charge to another phosphorylated STAT.

6. Phosphorylated STAT3 proteins then dimerise and enter the nucleus.

7. In the nucleus the dimer activates transcription of genes that induce inflammation. It does this as a transcription factor: the activated transcription regulator binds to specific regulatory DNA sequences and recruits RNA polymerase, or promotes assembly of the transcription initiation complex, resulting in transcription of the target gene. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 2 LO 2(i): transcriptional control by activators at control elements]

8. The mRNA is then translated, so the cell makes more of the proteins those genes encode. This is the third stage of cell signalling as LO 3(m) words it, a change in gene expression, meaning turning specific genes on or off and hence synthesis of enzymes or other proteins. Note that the target genes induce inflammation, they do not code for STAT3, and note that an examiner comment records students misinterpreting STAT3 target genes that induce inflammation and wrongly explaining that the target genes code for STAT3.

(b) The same rise in cyclic AMP concentration occurs in a liver cell and in a heart muscle cell, and the two cells do different things. Account for that, and decide at which of the three stages of cell signalling the difference must lie. [8]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Same rise in cyclic AMP, two different cells, two different outcomes. [8]

1. First, remove the wrong explanation. Cyclic AMP is a second messenger and hence is a small intracellular molecule that relays signals received by cell surface receptors to effectors. It is not a ligand and does not bind a cell surface receptor, so the difference cannot be that the two cells have different receptors for cyclic AMP. An examiner comment records that more than 40% of the students selected the wrong options, all of which made reference to cAMP acting as the ligand and thus binding to the cell surface receptor.

2. The correct explanation is the specificity argument. The specific combination of signalling proteins, including receptors, relay proteins in transduction pathways and proteins needed to carry out the response, gives a cell type specificity in both the signals it detects and the responses it produces.

3. So two cells that respond differently to the same signal differ in one or more of the proteins that receive, transduce and/or respond to the signal, which happens because different human cells contain different genes that are expressed, so the two cells carry different relay and response proteins. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 2 LO 2(i): differential gene expression is why two cells of one organism carry different protein sets]

4. The difference cannot lie at reception. Cyclic AMP is downstream of the receptor, and the stem fixes the cyclic AMP concentration as the same in both cells, so whatever happens at the receptor has already happened identically as far as this point.

5. It must lie at transduction, at the response, or at both. At transduction, the cells may hold different relay proteins sensitive to the cytosolic concentration of second messengers, so the cascades below cyclic AMP differ. Cyclic AMP's immediate effect is usually activation of protein kinase A, which then phosphorylates other proteins depending on the cell type.

6. At the response, the cells hold different proteins needed to carry out the response, so even an identical protein kinase A ends on different substrate proteins. A liver cell holds glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase, so its response is a change in cell metabolism, that is, regulation of enzyme activity; a cell whose kinase reaches the nucleus gives a change in gene expression instead.

7. The general statement of the argument, and the one worth memorising: human cells express different cell surface receptors that bind to the same ligand, or the same receptor that binds to the same ligand, with different relay proteins, activating different responses in each cell. In this case the second half of that sentence is what applies.

8. The same logic answers the reverse case. Different types of cells will result in different cellular responses when the same ligand binds to the cell due to difference in proteins present in each cell, and a single ligand can activate different cell types simultaneously, which is why one hormone in the blood can coordinate several tissues at once.

Sources & concepts

Source: School Prelim 2024 P3 Q1b(i) [2] and Q1b(ii) [5], also filed as HCI Prelim 2024 P3 Q1(b)(i) and Q1(b)(ii) (a, verbatim figure, marking points and both examiner comments, including the one on students thinking the target genes code for STAT3); RI Prelim 2024 P2 Q6(b)(i) [3] and Q6(b)(ii) [2] (a, the JAK cross-phosphorylation sequence and why phosphorylation allows STAT dimerisation, verbatim); NYJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q6a(iii) [3] (a, the events after kinase activation that produce a change in gene expression, verbatim); MJC Prelim 2018 P2 Q6ai [2] (a, phosphorylation as the post-translational modification that activates STAT, verbatim); School Prelim 2024 P1 Q24, also HCI Prelim 2024 P1 Q24, key D, correct in 56.51% of the cohort (b, verbatim option D and the examiner comment on cAMP being treated as a ligand); DHS Prelim 2021 P2 Q8c [2] (b, different relay molecules and second messengers giving different transduction pathways and responses, verbatim); TJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q10a [3] (b, different cell types giving different responses to the same ligand, verbatim); RVHS Prelim 2023 P3 Q1f [1] (b, simultaneous activation of different cell types by a single ligand, verbatim). The three-stage localisation in (b) is the extension. [INFERRED: extension, no official key] for that step. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain on a figure, then an explain question with a diagnosis attached, which is LO 3(m iii) tested as the outcome words it. Trap: treating cyclic AMP as a ligand for a cell surface receptor, which caught over 40% of the cohort. Second trap: answering (a) without ever reaching transcription, so the answer stops at the STAT3 dimer and never says that the cellular response is a change in gene expression. Concepts fused: (1) a hydrophilic ligand that cannot reach the nucleus; (2) receptor dimerisation and JAK cross-phosphorylation; (3) phosphotyrosines as docking sites; (4) phosphorylation changing conformation so two STAT molecules become complementary to each other; (5) dimerisation and nuclear entry; (6) a transcription factor binding a regulatory sequence and recruiting RNA polymerase, from Book 2; (7) the cellular response worded as a change in gene expression; (8) cyclic AMP as a second messenger and not a ligand; (9) specificity from the combination of receiving, transducing and responding proteins; (10) differential gene expression as the reason two cells hold different protein sets; (11) locating a difference at a named stage of a three-stage process; (12) cytoplasmic response against nuclear response.
